page_meta.description: Get seasonal allergy treatment online in California. Board-certified Family Medicine MD. CA telehealth law compliant. Aetna in-network. Self pay $49. AAAAI/ACAAI + ARIA-EAACI 2026 guidelines. Antihistamines, nasal steroids, immunotherapy referral.

opener.text: California adults with seasonal allergic rhinitis can receive evaluation and prescription allergy treatment — including intranasal corticosteroids, antihistamines, leukotriene receptor antagonists, and nasal antihistamine/steroid combinations — by secure video visit through TeleDirectMD, consistent with California Business and Professions Code Section 2290.5. A California-licensed board-certified Family Medicine physician reviews your allergen trigger history, symptom pattern, prior treatment response, and comorbid conditions (asthma, allergic conjunctivitis). AAAAI, ACAAI, and the updated ARIA-EAACI 2026 guidelines inform treatment selection. California's year-round pollen seasons — driven by dry chaparral, oak, and grass pollen in the Central Valley and Bay Area — create one of the highest seasonal allergy burdens in the U.S. Self pay is $49. Aetna is in-network effective April 30, 2026.

epidemiology.ca_prevalence: Allergic rhinitis affects approximately 19% of U.S. adults — an estimated 7.4 million California adults. California's Mediterranean climate with distinct wet and dry seasons, combined with its chaparral scrubland, grass plains in the Central Valley, and extensive urban tree plantings, creates pollen seasons that overlap year-round. Unlike much of the U.S., California does not have a defined allergy-free winter for most residents.

pollen_seasons.spring: February–June: tree pollen (oak, alder, ash, birch, cedar/juniper) — peaks in Sacramento Valley and Bay Area
pollen_seasons.summer: May–October: grass pollen (bermuda, timothy, fescue) — dominant in California's Central Valley, one of the highest grass pollen counts in the nation
pollen_seasons.fall: July–November: weed pollen (sagebrush, mugwort, plantain) — significant in Southern California chaparral; ragweed less prevalent than eastern U.S.
pollen_seasons.wildfire: Wildfire smoke (year-round risk 2020–present) exacerbates allergic rhinitis and asthma symptoms independent of pollen season

epidemiology.ca_specific: The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) tracks seasonal allergy-related primary care visits. The Central Valley Bioaerosol Network and Bay Area Air Quality Management District (BAAQMD) publish real-time pollen count data. California's agricultural activity (almond, pistachio, citrus orchards) contributes to occupational pollen exposure for farmworkers.

clinical_guidelines.primary: AAAAI/ACAAI + ARIA (Allergic Rhinitis and Its Impact on Asthma) 2026 update + EAACI 2026

stepwise_treatment.mild_intermittent: OTC oral antihistamine (loratadine, cetirizine, fexofenadine) PRN — no daily therapy needed
stepwise_treatment.mild_persistent: Daily intranasal corticosteroid (INCS) — first-line per ARIA 2026; most effective monotherapy for nasal congestion and overall symptom control
stepwise_treatment.moderate_severe: INCS + oral antihistamine; consider adding oral montelukast (LTRA), intranasal antihistamine (azelastine), or nasal antihistamine/ICS combination spray (Dymista)
stepwise_treatment.inadequate_control: Consider allergen immunotherapy referral (subcutaneous or sublingual) — only disease-modifying therapy for allergic rhinitis

clinical_guidelines.incs_preference: INCS is the most effective single agent for allergic rhinitis per ARIA 2026 — reduces nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, sneezing, and nasal pruritus. Preferred over antihistamine monotherapy for moderate-severe or persistent symptoms. Minimal systemic absorption with recommended doses.
clinical_guidelines.antihistamine_guidance: Second-generation antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine, levocetirizine, desloratadine) preferred over first-generation (diphenhydramine) due to non-sedating profile. Fexofenadine has least sedation; cetirizine may cause mild sedation.
clinical_guidelines.ltra_note: Montelukast for allergic rhinitis carries an FDA boxed warning for neuropsychiatric events — should not be used as first-line when safer alternatives are effective.
clinical_guidelines.immunotherapy_referral: Allergen immunotherapy (SCIT or SLIT) is the only disease-modifying treatment and is indicated for: moderate-severe allergic rhinitis not adequately controlled by pharmacotherapy, patient preference for reduced medication dependence, comorbid allergic asthma, and when desensitization to specific allergens is feasible. TeleDirectMD facilitates referral to allergist for immunotherapy evaluation.
clinical_guidelines.monitoring: Annual review of allergen trigger list, symptom control, medication tolerance, and immunotherapy progress. Pollen count awareness counseling (BAAQMD, California DPR pollen data resources).

medications.name: Fluticasone propionate nasal spray 50 mcg (Flonase, generic)
medications.regimen: 2 sprays each nostril once daily; 1 spray maintenance
medications.notes: First-line for moderate-persistent allergic rhinitis per ARIA 2026. Minimal systemic absorption. Also available as Flonase Sensimist (aqueous mist, less drip).

medications.name: Mometasone nasal spray 50 mcg (Nasonex, generic)
medications.notes: Similar efficacy to fluticasone. Generic available.

medications.name: Budesonide nasal spray 32 mcg (Rhinocort, generic)
medications.notes: Gentle aqueous formulation, well-tolerated. Good choice for patients prone to nasal dryness.

medications.name: Cetirizine (Zyrtec) 10 mg
medications.notes: Low sedation, rapid onset. May cause mild drowsiness in some patients.

medications.name: Fexofenadine (Allegra) 180 mg
medications.regimen: 180 mg once daily or 60 mg BID
medications.notes: Least sedating antihistamine. Best choice for daytime use when driving or operating machinery.

medications.name: Loratadine (Claritin) 10 mg
medications.notes: Non-sedating. Generic widely available in California pharmacies.

medications.name: Azelastine/fluticasone nasal spray (Dymista)
medications.notes: FDA-approved combination for moderate-severe allergic rhinitis inadequately controlled by INCS alone. Provides antihistamine and steroid effects in a single spray.

faqs.question: Can I get seasonal allergy treatment online in California?
faqs.answer: Yes. California Business and Professions Code Section 2290.5 permits licensed physicians to deliver care via synchronous video telehealth without a prior in-person visit. TeleDirectMD's California-licensed board-certified Family Medicine physician evaluates your symptom pattern, allergen triggers, and prior treatment response before prescribing intranasal corticosteroids, antihistamines, leukotriene receptor antagonists, or combination nasal sprays. Self pay is $49; Aetna is in-network effective April 30, 2026.

faqs.question: What makes California allergy seasons different from the rest of the U.S.?
faqs.answer: California's Mediterranean climate creates a nearly year-round pollen season with no true winter respite for most residents. Tree pollen peaks from February through June, grass pollen (including bermuda and timothy from the Central Valley, which has some of the highest grass pollen counts in the nation) runs from May through October, and weed pollen persists from July through November. Wildfire smoke — now a year-round risk — worsens allergic rhinitis and asthma symptoms independent of pollen counts. The Bay Area Air Quality Management District (BAAQMD) publishes real-time pollen data relevant to Northern California residents.

faqs.question: What is the first-line treatment for seasonal allergies per ARIA 2026?
faqs.answer: The ARIA 2026 (Allergic Rhinitis and Its Impact on Asthma) updated guideline and AAAAI/ACAAI practice parameters establish intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) as the most effective first-line treatment for persistent or moderate-severe allergic rhinitis. INCS — including fluticasone propionate (Flonase), mometasone (Nasonex), and budesonide (Rhinocort) — reduce nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, sneezing, and nasal pruritus more effectively than oral antihistamines alone. For mild intermittent symptoms, second-generation antihistamines (cetirizine, fexofenadine, loratadine) are appropriate as monotherapy.

faqs.question: What allergy medications are safe and non-sedating for California adults who drive?
faqs.answer: Second-generation antihistamines are the appropriate choice for Californians who drive or work heavy equipment. Fexofenadine (Allegra 180 mg) is the least sedating second-generation antihistamine and is the preferred choice for daytime drivers. Loratadine (Claritin 10 mg) is also non-sedating. Cetirizine (Zyrtec 10 mg) may cause mild sedation in some patients. Avoid first-generation antihistamines (diphenhydramine/Benadryl, chlorpheniramine) — these cause significant sedation and are contraindicated when driving. Intranasal corticosteroids do not cause sedation.

faqs.question: How much do prescription allergy medications cost in California with GoodRx?
faqs.answer: Many allergy medications are available over the counter or as affordable generics. Fluticasone nasal spray (generic Flonase): available OTC approximately $15–$25 per month. Mometasone nasal spray (generic Nasonex): approximately $15–$30 per month with GoodRx. Cetirizine, loratadine, and fexofenadine are available OTC at approximately $8–$20 per month generic. The combination nasal spray (azelastine/fluticasone/Dymista) runs approximately $100–$200 per bottle — manufacturer savings programs available.

faqs.question: What is allergen immunotherapy and can TeleDirectMD prescribe it?
faqs.answer: Allergen immunotherapy (SCIT: subcutaneous immunotherapy — allergy shots; SLIT: sublingual immunotherapy — drops or tablets) is the only disease-modifying treatment for allergic rhinitis — it builds tolerance to specific allergens and can produce lasting symptom reduction after treatment is completed. TeleDirectMD can facilitate a referral to a California allergist for immunotherapy evaluation. Administering allergen immunotherapy requires an in-person allergist, but TeleDirectMD can provide prescription antihistamines, nasal steroids, and symptom management while you pursue immunotherapy.

faqs.question: Does California wildfire smoke worsen seasonal allergies?
faqs.answer: Yes. California wildfire smoke significantly worsens allergic rhinitis and asthma symptoms. Wildfire smoke contains fine particulate matter (PM2.5), volatile organic compounds, and combustion byproducts that directly irritate nasal mucosa and trigger allergic inflammation independent of pollen. During smoke events — tracked by the California Air Resources Board (CARB) — the physician may recommend temporary dose increase of intranasal corticosteroids, indoor air filtration (HEPA filter), N95 mask use outdoors, and asthma action plan review for patients with comorbid asthma.

faqs.question: What is the FDA warning for montelukast in seasonal allergies?
faqs.answer: The FDA issued a boxed warning for montelukast (Singulair) in 2020 for serious neuropsychiatric adverse events including agitation, aggression, depression, suicidal ideation, and suicidality. Because effective alternatives (intranasal corticosteroids, antihistamines) exist for allergic rhinitis, the FDA recommends against prescribing montelukast as first-line therapy for allergic rhinitis when alternatives are appropriate. TeleDirectMD prescribes montelukast for allergic rhinitis only when other options have failed or are contraindicated, and discusses the boxed warning with patients before prescribing.

faqs.question: Does California insurance cover allergy treatment visits?
faqs.answer: California Assembly Bill 744 (2019) requires commercial health plans to reimburse telehealth allergy management visits on the same basis as in-person care. Aetna commercial is in-network with TeleDirectMD in California effective April 30, 2026; UnitedHealthcare Commercial is approved effective May 29, 2026. Anthem Blue Cross and Cigna are pending enrollment. Many allergy medications (fluticasone, cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine) are also available over the counter without a prescription in California pharmacies.

faqs.question: When do seasonal allergies require in-person evaluation instead of telehealth?
faqs.answer: Seek in-person evaluation for: severe allergic reaction or anaphylaxis after allergen exposure (use EpiPen + call 911); new nasal polyps, orbital cellulitis, or sinusitis with high fever; suspected allergic fungal sinusitis; first-time evaluation for allergen immunotherapy; or when multiple treatments have failed and allergy skin testing or immunoCap testing is needed to identify specific triggers. TeleDirectMD manages symptom-based allergic rhinitis without requiring skin testing for established allergen patterns.

faqs.question: Can TeleDirectMD treat children's seasonal allergies in California?
faqs.answer: TeleDirectMD treats adults 18 years of age and older only. Children with seasonal allergies should be seen by their pediatrician, a board-certified allergist, or a pediatric primary care provider. Pediatric allergy resources in California include the AAAAI Find an Allergist tool at aaaai.org and Medi-Cal managed care pediatric providers for insured children.

faqs.question: What should I track before my seasonal allergy visit with TeleDirectMD?
faqs.answer: Before your visit, note: which months your symptoms are worst (helps identify tree vs. grass vs. weed pollen dominance); symptom severity score (nasal congestion, runny nose, sneezing, itchy eyes — 0–3 scale); what treatments you have tried (including OTC antihistamines, nasal sprays) and how well they worked; comorbid conditions (asthma, eczema, food allergies, nasal polyps, sinus infections); and any occupational exposures (agricultural work, outdoor labor in the Central Valley). This history helps the physician select the most effective treatment from the start.
